category: 67. RWF-004a: a package whose public facade DECLARES NOTHING and assembles module.exports entirely from require()d siblings inside the same installed package
description: vt2-vuln-lib's index.js declares no functions at all: it does `var ops = require('./internal/ops')` and exports `{ dangerousOp: ops.dangerousOp, ... }`, where ./internal/ops.js is itself `module.exports = require('../impl')` -- so the real dangerousOp sits two same-package re-export hops from the name the application calls. This is the dominant authoring pattern for any CommonJS package past trivial size (qs, semver and debug all do it) and is the exact shape of RWF-004a. Three traps are layered on top: (a) the same package contains unused.js, which declares an identically-named dangerousOp that nothing exports -- a bare same-package name search binds there; (b) the facade also re-exports a DIFFERENT installed package's identically-named dangerousOp as `borrowedOp`, so a chase that ignores package identity can wander into vt2-decoy-lib; (c) safeOp travels the identical mechanism and is never called, so a mechanism that resolves the relation but loses track of which name it resolved would flag the wrong symbol. The application calls only lib.dangerousOp(userInput), directly and unconditionally.
reason: main() passes userInput straight into lib.dangerousOp(), and lib.dangerousOp IS vt2-vuln-lib's own impl.js dangerousOp -- reached through two statically-written, literal-specifier require() hops that never leave the installed package. A human analyst reading index.js, internal/ops.js and impl.js together has no ambiguity: the call lands on the exact function GHSA-vt2v2-0001 names, in this exact installed instance. Neither the never-exported decoy in unused.js nor vt2-decoy-lib's same-named function is on that path, and neither may be substituted for it.

category: 68. RWF-003: a package whose entire public API is an ANONYMOUS function assigned to module.exports, reached through a same-package facade that declares nothing
description: vt2-vuln-lib's whole callable API is `module.exports = function (input) {...}` -- an anonymous function expression with no name anywhere to match on -- sitting two same-package re-export hops behind a facade that declares nothing (`index.js: module.exports = require('./internal/ops')`, `ops.js: module.exports = require('../impl')`). This is the shape of real minimist@1.2.5 and of qs's lib/parse.js and lib/stringify.js. Three traps are layered on top: (a) impl.js declares a named `dangerousOp` BEFORE the real export that nothing exports, where both a same-file name search and a 'first function in the file' heuristic land; (b) the same package contains unused.js, a SECOND anonymous module.exports function that nothing requires and nothing re-exports, so a mechanism binding 'an anonymous exported function in this package' rather than the one the chain reaches would pick the wrong node; (c) the facade hangs a DIFFERENT installed package's identically-shaped anonymous export off its own exported value as `borrowed`, so a chase that ignores package identity can wander into vt2-decoy-lib. The application calls only lib(userInput), directly and unconditionally.
reason: main() passes userInput straight into lib(), and lib IS vt2-vuln-lib's own impl.js anonymous function -- reached through two statically-written, literal-specifier require() hops that never leave the installed package. A human analyst reading index.js, internal/ops.js and impl.js together has no ambiguity: the call lands on the exact function GHSA-vt2v2-0001 names, in this exact installed instance. The function having no name changes nothing about that: its identity is its position in impl.js. Neither the never-exported named decoy, nor the never-required second anonymous export in unused.js, nor vt2-decoy-lib's same-shaped function is on that path, and none may be substituted for it.

category: 69. RWF-013: a CommonJS export through a variable whose SAFE initializer is reassigned to the vulnerable implementation before the export runs
description: vt2-vuln-lib/index.js declares `let dangerousOp = function (input) {...}` -- a safe pure-JS fallback -- then conditionally replaces it with the native addon (`if (process.env.VT2_NATIVE === '1') { dangerousOp = require('./native'); }`) and only then writes `exports.dangerousOp = dangerousOp`. The export carries the VARIABLE's value at export time, not the function expression that merely initialized it. The trap has two halves that only bite together: (a) the stale initializer is ANONYMOUS, so source indexing names it after the variable it was assigned to, giving a name-based export attribution a perfect same-file match under the exact export name the advisory asks for; and (b) native.js's real implementation is anonymous too (`module.exports = function (input) {...}`), so the stale fallback is the ONLY thing in the entire installed package carrying the name 'dangerousOp' -- there is no correct same-named node anywhere for the target sweep to prefer. The package also publishes the real implementation under a second, statically resolvable name (`exports.dangerousOpNative = require('./native')`), and the application calls THAT one unconditionally. So the call graph correctly reaches native.js's function while the rule target, bound by name, lands on the stale fallback in index.js -- a node nothing calls. Proving that node unreachable then yields a confident NOT_AFFECTED about a function the package may well never export.
reason: A human analyst reading index.js cannot decide what `exports.dangerousOp` holds: it is the safe fallback or native.js's function depending on `process.env.VT2_NATIVE`, which the analyst is not given. If the addon branch ran, `dangerousOp` and `dangerousOpNative` are the SAME function object and main() passes userInput straight into it, so the vulnerability cannot be ruled out; if it did not, the safe fallback is exported and never called, so neither can it be confirmed. NOT_AFFECTED is the one answer that is definitely unjustified: it is reachable only by treating the stale initializer as the export's identity, which discards the reassignment the file plainly performs.
vulnerableTarget: vt2-vuln-lib#dangerousOp (whatever value the export holds after the conditional reassignment)

category: 70. RWF-013b: a CommonJS export through a FUNCTION DECLARATION that is reassigned to the vulnerable implementation before the export runs
description: The sibling of ADV2-069, differing in exactly one respect that turns out to decide soundness: the stale binding is a FUNCTION DECLARATION rather than a `let` initializer. vt2-vuln-lib/index.js declares `function dangerousOp(input) {...}` -- a safe pure-JS fallback -- conditionally replaces it with the native addon (`if (process.env.VT2_NATIVE === '1') { dangerousOp = require('./native'); }`), and only then writes `exports.dangerousOp = dangerousOp`. RWF-013 closed this defect for `var`/`let`/`const` bindings by classifying an identifier's provenance from HOW IT WAS DECLARED, so a reassigned function declaration -- which JavaScript rebinds just as freely -- was reported 'unmodeled' and still fell through to the legacy name search. Here that search has an even easier target than ADV2-069's: the declaration is literally named `dangerousOp`, requiring no name inference at all, and native.js's real implementation is anonymous, so the stale declaration is the ONLY thing in the entire installed package carrying that name. The package publishes the real implementation under a second, statically resolvable name, which the application calls -- so the call graph reaches native.js correctly while the rule target binds to a declaration nothing calls.
reason: A human analyst reading index.js cannot decide what `exports.dangerousOp` holds: it is the safe declaration or native.js's function depending on `process.env.VT2_NATIVE`, which the analyst is not given. If that branch ran, `dangerousOp` and `dangerousOpNative` are the SAME function object and main() passes userInput straight into it, so the vulnerability cannot be ruled out; if it did not, the safe fallback is exported and never called, so neither can it be confirmed. NOT_AFFECTED is the one answer that is definitely unjustified: it is reachable only by treating the stale declaration as the export's identity, which discards a reassignment the file performs in plain sight. That the binding happens to be a function declaration rather than a variable changes nothing a reader would conclude, and so must change nothing the analyzer concludes.
vulnerableTarget: vt2-vuln-lib#dangerousOp (whatever value the export holds after the conditional reassignment)
